books.name: The Great Escape
books.focus: dashes and brackets: an aside opens and closes with the same mark

items.s: The octopus—a master of disguise___ slipped out of its tank overnight.
items.tip: An aside that opens with a dash closes with a dash.

no.,: The aside opened with a dash, so it must close with a dash. A dash and a comma don't make a pair.
no.): A closing bracket needs an opening bracket, but this aside opened with a dash.
no.;: A semicolon would cut the sentence in two, and 'The octopus, a master of disguise' isn't a full sentence.

items.say: The octopus—a master of disguise—slipped out of its tank overnight.
items.ask: The octopus—a master of disguise slipped out of its tank overnight.

items.s: There was only one suspect___ Inky the octopus.
items.tip: A dash (or a colon) leads to a surprise or an answer at the end of a sentence.

no.,: A comma is too weak to build up to the big reveal. Use a dash or a colon.
no.;: A semicolon needs a full sentence after it, but Inky the octopus isn't one.
no.no mark: Without a mark, the reveal runs straight on from the sentence.

items.say: There was only one suspect—Inky the octopus.
items.ask: There was only one suspect Inky the octopus.

items.s: The keepers (who had searched every corner___ finally found Inky in a drainpipe.
items.tip: An aside that opens with a bracket closes with a bracket.

no.—: The aside opened with a bracket, so it must close with a bracket, not a dash.
no.,: A bracket can't be closed by a comma.
no.no mark: The bracket was opened, so it must be closed before the sentence goes on.

items.say: The keepers (who had searched every corner) finally found Inky in a drainpipe.
items.ask: The keepers (who had searched every corner finally found Inky in a drainpipe.

items.s: Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood and nine brains___ or so the guide claimed.
items.tip: A dash adds an afterthought at the end of a sentence.

no.;: A semicolon needs a full sentence after it. or so the guide claimed isn't one.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation or list, not an afterthought.
no.!: ! would end the sentence, and or starts with a small o.

items.say: Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood and nine brains—or so the guide claimed.
items.ask: Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood and nine brains or so the guide claimed.

items.s: Inky's favourite toy (a plastic crab___ was found next to him.
items.tip: Brackets come in pairs: (a plastic crab).

no.—: The aside opened with a bracket, so it closes with a bracket.
no.,: A comma can't close a bracket.
no.no mark: The bracket is still open. Close it before was found.

items.say: Inky's favourite toy (a plastic crab) was found next to him.
items.ask: Inky's favourite toy (a plastic crab was found next to him.

items.s: The aquarium has one strict rule___ never tap on the glass.
items.tip: A colon (or a dash) introduces what the rule is.

no.,: A comma is too weak to introduce the rule.
no.;: A semicolon needs two full sentences. Here the second part explains the rule, which is a colon's job.
no.no mark: Without a mark, the rule crashes into the sentence.

items.say: The aquarium has one strict rule: never tap on the glass.
items.ask: The aquarium has one strict rule never tap on the glass.

items.s: Some visitors___ especially the younger ones—pressed their noses to the tank.
items.tip: The aside closes with a dash, so it must open with a dash.

no.,: The aside closes with a dash (ones—pressed), so it must open with a dash, not a comma.
no.(: A bracket would need a closing bracket, but the aside closes with a dash.
no.;: A semicolon would cut off Some visitors, which isn't a full sentence.

items.say: Some visitors—especially the younger ones—pressed their noses to the tank.
items.ask: Some visitors especially the younger ones—pressed their noses to the tank.

items.s: The story went viral___ by Monday, millions had watched the video.
items.tip: Two full sentences can be joined with a semicolon (or, less formally, a dash).

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences (a comma splice).
no.): There's no opening bracket, so there's nothing to close.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.

items.say: The story went viral; by Monday, millions had watched the video.
items.ask: The story went viral by Monday, millions had watched the video.

books.name: Hyphens that Help
books.focus: describing words joined before a noun (a ten-year-old) · no hyphens after the verb

items.s: My ___ cousin can already write code.
items.tip: Words that describe a noun together are joined by hyphens: a ten-year-old cousin.

no.ten year old: When three words describe the cousin together, join them with hyphens: ten-year-old.
no.ten-year old: All three words work as one describing word, so both hyphens are needed.
no.ten-years-old: Before a noun the number word stays singular: a ten-year-old, not ten-years-old.

items.say: My ten-year-old cousin can already write code.
items.ask: My ten-year-old cousin can already write code.

items.s: My cousin is ten ___.
items.tip: After the verb (is ten years old), there are no hyphens and years is plural.

no.years-old: After the verb, years old isn't joined by a hyphen. Hyphens are for describing words before a noun.
no.year-old: year-old needs a noun after it (a ten-year-old girl). Here we say ten years old.
no.year's old: There's no apostrophe here: ten years old.

items.say: My cousin is ten years old.
items.ask: My cousin is ten years old.

items.s: The final was a ___ match.
items.tip: Two words that describe a noun together are joined by a hyphen: a nail-biting match.

no.nail biting: nail biting before match reads like two separate things. Join them: nail-biting.
no.nailbiting: This word is written with a hyphen: nail-biting.
no.nail-bitting: The spelling is biting (one t): nail-biting.

items.say: The final was a nail-biting match.
items.ask: The final was a nail-biting match.

items.s: We need a ___ plan for the science fair.
items.tip: A long describing phrase before a noun is joined with hyphens: a well-thought-out plan.

no.well thought out: Before the noun, the three words work as one describing word, so they're joined: well-thought-out.
no.well-thought out: All three words belong together, so both hyphens are needed.
no.wellthoughtout: These words are joined by hyphens, not squashed into one.

items.say: We need a well-thought-out plan for the science fair.
items.ask: We need a well-thought-out plan for the science fair.

items.s: The new tablet has a ___ battery.
items.tip: long-lasting describes the battery as one idea, so it takes a hyphen.

no.long lasting: Before a noun, long and lasting work as one describing word, so join them: long-lasting.
no.longlasting: This is written with a hyphen: long-lasting.
no.long-lastting: The spelling is lasting (one t): long-lasting.

items.say: The new tablet has a long-lasting battery.
items.ask: The new tablet has a long-lasting battery.

items.s: Beware of the ___ plants in the greenhouse!
items.tip: insect-eating = plants that eat insects. The hyphen joins the two describing words.

no.insect eating: Without the hyphen it reads like an insect that is eating plants! Join them: insect-eating.
no.insects-eating: In a describing word the noun stays singular: insect-eating.
no.insecteating: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.

items.say: Beware of the insect-eating plants in the greenhouse!
items.ask: Beware of the insect-eating plants in the greenhouse!

items.s: We watched a ___ film about penguins.
items.tip: A number + a measure before a noun is hyphenated and singular: a two-hour film.

no.two hour: Before a noun, the number and the measure are joined: a two-hour film.
no.two-hours: Before a noun the measure stays singular: two-hour, not two-hours.
no.twohour: These words are joined by a hyphen, not squashed into one.

items.say: We watched a two-hour film about penguins.
items.ask: We watched a two-hour film about penguins.

items.s: Grandma has surprisingly ___ ideas about video games.
items.tip: Before a noun, up-to-date is joined with hyphens: up-to-date ideas.

no.up to date: Before the noun (ideas), the phrase works as one describing word, so it takes hyphens.
no.uptodate: These words are joined by hyphens, not squashed into one.
no.up-to date: All three words belong together, so both hyphens are needed.

items.say: Grandma has surprisingly up-to-date ideas about video games.
items.ask: Grandma has surprisingly up-to-date ideas about video games.

books.name: The School Paper
books.focus: semicolons instead of comma splices · semicolons in a list of lists · colons

items.s: Our paper needed a new editor___ however, nobody volunteered.
items.tip: Before however joining two sentences, use a semicolon (or a full stop and a capital H).

no.,: A comma before however can't join two full sentences (a comma splice).
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but nobody volunteering doesn't explain the first part.
A full stop works only with a capital: However. Here however has a small h.

items.say: Our paper needed a new editor; however, nobody volunteered.
items.ask: Our paper needed a new editor however, nobody volunteered.

items.s: We interviewed Ms Ong, the coach___ Mr Raj, the librarian; and Lily, the captain.
items.tip: When the things in a list already have commas, split the list items with semicolons.

no.,: Each item already has a comma inside it (Ms Ong, the coach), so commas between items would be confusing.
no.:: A colon introduces a list. It doesn't split the items.
no.—: A dash would add an aside, but here we need to split the list items, as the later semicolon does.

items.say: We interviewed Ms Ong, the coach; Mr Raj, the librarian; and Lily, the captain.
items.ask: We interviewed Ms Ong, the coach Mr Raj, the librarian; and Lily, the captain.

items.s: The deadline was Friday___ we finished on Thursday night.
items.tip: Two full, linked sentences can be joined with a semicolon.

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.
A full stop works only with a capital: We finished… Here we has a small w.

items.say: The deadline was Friday; we finished on Thursday night.
items.ask: The deadline was Friday we finished on Thursday night.

items.s: One headline caused a stir___ Canteen Bans Chips!
items.tip: A colon introduces the thing you've been talking about: the headline itself.

no.;: A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides, and it can't introduce the headline.
no.,: A comma is too weak to introduce the headline.
no.no mark: Without a mark, the headline crashes into the sentence.

items.say: One headline caused a stir: Canteen Bans Chips!
items.ask: One headline caused a stir Canteen Bans Chips!

items.s: The article was funny___ moreover, it was true.
items.tip: Linking words like moreover and therefore join two sentences after a semicolon.

no.,: A comma before moreover can't join two full sentences.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but it was true doesn't explain why it was funny.
A full stop works only with a capital: Moreover. Here moreover has a small m.

items.say: The article was funny; moreover, it was true.
items.ask: The article was funny moreover, it was true.

items.s: We had a problem___ the printer was out of ink.
items.tip: A colon (or a dash) introduces the explanation: what was the problem?

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.
no.?: This isn't a question. It tells us there was a problem.

items.say: We had a problem: the printer was out of ink.
items.ask: We had a problem the printer was out of ink.

items.s: Readers loved the puzzle page___ in fact, it was the most popular part.
items.tip: Before in fact joining two sentences, use a semicolon.

no.,: A comma before in fact can't join two full sentences.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.

items.say: Readers loved the puzzle page; in fact, it was the most popular part.
items.ask: Readers loved the puzzle page in fact, it was the most popular part.

items.s: The editor's decision was clear___ from next term, the paper would come out every week.
items.tip: A colon introduces what the decision was.

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences, and it can't introduce the decision.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.
no.?: This isn't a question. It tells us the decision.

items.say: The editor's decision was clear: from next term, the paper would come out every week.
items.ask: The editor's decision was clear from next term, the paper would come out every week.
